name: Balancing Feedback Loop
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: The Loop That Pulls Systems Back to Earth
lesson.summary: A balancing feedback loop is a closed causal chain with an odd number of negative links, which makes it self-correcting: it resists change and pulls a system back toward a goal or equilibrium rather than amplifying whatever push it receives.
lesson.body:
A balancing feedback loop is the mirror image of a reinforcing one. Trace the arrows all the way around a balancing loop and count the minus signs, and if that count is odd, you have a balancing loop, conventionally labeled B on a diagram. Where a reinforcing loop amplifies whatever change it receives, a balancing loop opposes it. Push a balancing loop's variable up and the loop pushes back down, push it down and the loop pushes back up. This is what makes balancing loops goal seeking: they behave as though they are trying to reach and hold some target value, even when no single component of the loop has any explicit goal of its own.

The textbook example is a thermostat. Room temperature drops below the setpoint, the thermostat turns the heater on, the heater raises the temperature, and once the temperature reaches the setpoint the thermostat turns the heater off again. In practice the easiest way to recognize a balancing loop is not to count signs but to look for a goal, a measurement of the gap to that goal, and an action that shrinks the gap. That structure, comparison to a target followed by a corrective action, is the intuitive signature of balance regardless of exactly how the signs work out.

Quantum computing has candidate balancing loops of its own, though this book will spend real time asking whether they are strong enough to matter. Peer review is meant to be one: an overstated claim invites scrutiny, scrutiny that holds up produces corrections or retractions, and corrections restore the field's credibility, damping down the next round of overstatement. Physical decoherence is another, in a different sense: no matter how much excitement or funding a research program generates, qubits still lose coherence at a rate set by physics, not by press coverage, and that rate acts as a hard ceiling on how fast real capability can actually advance, regardless of how fast the reinforcing hype loop is spinning.

Most real systems, quantum computing very much included, are not pure reinforcing loops or pure balancing loops but a tangle of both operating on the same variables at once. Which behavior dominates, sustained exponential change or a return to some equilibrium, depends on the relative strength of the loops, not on which type is theoretically present. A weak balancing loop attached to a strong reinforcing loop gets overpowered and barely slows the trend, while a strong balancing loop can keep a powerful reinforcing loop pinned near its starting point almost indefinitely, the way a thermostat holds a room steady regardless of outdoor temperature swings.

This sets up one of the central diagnostic questions running through the skeptical chapters ahead. If quantum computing's public narrative is dominated by a reinforcing hype loop, as the next chapter will argue in detail, the natural follow up question is whether an adequately strong balancing loop exists anywhere in the system to keep that hype tethered to actual physical progress. That question turns out to be genuinely contested, and it is worth holding onto as you read the chapters on hype, sunk costs, and the geopolitical funding race that follow.
